utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before I give you an opportunity, Mr. Misetic, to continue your cross-examination, there are a few procedural matters which I would like to deal with very quickly, the first one in private session. Mrs. Rehn, you'll not know what I'm talking about anyhow, so, therefore, there's no need to ask you to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. There was a request to know as quickly as possible about the documents filed in relation to Mrs. Rehn by the Prosecution. Therefore, looking at the list provided by Mr. Registrar, where he gives a total survey of all the pending bar table requests, starting at number 142. I don't know whether you have that list at hand. The first one, 142, was already in evidence. That was D669, so that is clear; the second one, 2710, was already admitted into evidence as P639, if I'm not mistaken, Ms. Mahindaratne; then number 147, 4312, was admitted into evidence, under seal, as P643. What then remains is 144, which is 65 ter 2820; 145, which is 4102; 146, which is 4128; we dealt already with 147; 148, 4332. I do understand that there's no need for confidentiality here, so that this is a mistake that the confidential box is -- yes, it can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is as a public document. Then we have 149, 4367; 150, 4371; 151, 4394; 152, 4450; 153, 4453; 154 on this list is 65 ter 5318; and 155 is 3332.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear that although we discussed 4312, that no decision finally has been taken to admit this exhibit which appears as number 147 on the list. The Chamber admits into evidence the numbers I just mentioned, 144 up to and including 155; 147 is admitted under seal; all the other documents are admitted into evidence as public documents. The numbers were already assigned, that is, P640 up to and including P642, public; P643, under seal; P644 up to and including P651, all admitted as public exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just point out document number which is now marked as P650, that is, 65 ter number 5318, has been admitted on a previous occasion - I pointed that out yesterday - under Exhibit Number P477. I placed that on record yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I must have overlooked that, Ms. Mahindaratne. My apologies for that. Mr. Registrar, will we forget P650 and use that at a later stage, rather than now changing the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that that number will be skipped. Mrs. Rehn, this is not a bookkeeping session, but we have to deal with some formalities now and then. Apologies and thank you for your patience. May I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, again, Mrs. Rehn.

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would like to start this morning's session by taking you to page 2 of your statement - page 2 and 3, I should say - discussing some of the things that you say in your statement you personally observed. At the bottom paragraph on page 2, in the middle of the paragraph, you say: "These included a number of visits to Sector South. On these visits, I observed the Croatian military looting civilian property." If we could stop there. Do you recall where you saw Croatian military looting, in what town and when?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As told in my report and in the -- in the different notes that have been taken during the visits, there are several villages that I went to, and I can't recall the names. I'm very sorry for that. My first visit was together with two -- to the Sector North in 1995, October, together with two UNMOs, a Norwegian and a Kenyan. And they took me around to look at what was happening there on the ground. I visited some houses. There was a paralyzed woman who had been shot at through her window --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting. I think as a matter that Mr. Misetic is defending a case which is exclusively located in Sector South, so, therefore, just in terms of using our time --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Okay. Sorry. I understand that. Because for me, of course, this is a whole with what I have experienced. So, in Sector South, I went a few times to the town of Knin, to the villages around there that I can't mention. I can't remember the names. I'm sorry, but I'm very bad with names; it's good if I remember my own one. Therefore, I only have to state that it was during several visits. And I also want to remind you about the method of my work in minutes, in the reports we have mentioned, high-level persons, politicians, others I have met with. Although, the most people I met with were at a grass-roots level going in and out of houses, talking with both Croats and a few Serbs that were returning, and seeing what I saw. So these lootings were something I observed there around Knin and also in other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just so that we clarify this point. Is this something that you -- information you received from other people, or are you saying that you were present while you saw military people looting houses?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw military people looting houses; and as I have corrected afterwards in -- I think in my second statement, that, of course, I can't go on oath on that they were military because something I learned also in other parts of the former Yugoslavia was that clothes were used whenever you could get them. So it could be civilians that are having military uniforms. On the other hand, the vehicles were much pointing on the fact that it must have been, and it was in my mind quite clear that it should be military persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would that have been something that would have -- you would have put in one of your reports that you personally eye-witnessed military trucks with people looting --

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is already in some of the minutes that I saw this, and also in my statement, because all over you could see trucks where men were taking different items from houses, starting with windows and window frames and fridges and so on. So that was what happened on several occasions around -- when I was travelling around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But I'm not asking about the minutes of meetings or your witness statement here. I'm asking you in your reports to the Secretary-General, do you -- if you had personally eye-witnessed soldiers looting and military trucks present, that would be something important enough to include in one of your reports. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. And I must say that I believe that it is also stated, but perhaps it should have been, because we always talked in the "we" format: The UN, the units saw, and the staff saw, and so on. So we never pointed out especially my own role. I was one of "we."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if I could turn to your supplemental statement at paragraph 12, you say: "Almost every Serb house was vandalized with the word "Chetnik." Where was this?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Especially in Knin and there around. It was so clear, the hate, when I talked with Croatian people, the enormous hate to those who perhaps would be returning, the Serbs. They didn't want them to come back. And then as an opposite, on every Croat house, there was the Croat chequer-board flag showing that here are real people living.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So you have a personal memory of every house -- almost every Serb house in Knin having the word "Chetnik" written on it?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So many of these houses had it. It would be exaggeration to say that every house, because it was impossible for me to know which houses were left by Serbs. But too many of them had this red "Chetnik" on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you say: "I remember we had to be careful when going into the Serbian villages because we had been told of occasions when Serbian houses had been booby-trapped to blow up if the Serbs attempted to return." First, who gave you that information?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was given to me by, of course, my own staff - and when I'm talking about "my own staff," it is the staff of the United Nations Commission for Human Rights - but also by military I spoke with, and my security major that was from Finland who was following me and, of course, was very keen of my security. He thought that it would be not absolutely necessary for me to step into a booby-trap. So, therefore, he collected information from police, from military. And there was a clear warning. One house I went to I had to -- I was especially warned about because there had been a return by Serbs who were not allowed to go to the house. They had to live in the animals' hamlet together with some animals, and it was a nasty situation. But, of course, I went to that house but I was told to be very careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So you have -- you don't know whether houses were actually booby-trapped; this is something that was just told to you?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course, I couldn't, because if I would have stepped into one booby-trap, then I should have known that there is one. But I did not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you for examples. Did you subsequently receive any information that there was ever a house that had been booby-trapped --

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I got the information, and especially through my security advisor, that be careful because it has been told by UN staff that there have been booby-traps. And, of course, I met also with a couple who had moved in and got immediately a bomb, some grenade, something, thrown into their house. So the man was in hospital, and the woman had quite serious injuries when she told us about how lovely the neighbours are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Where was the booby-trapped -- where were the booby-trapped houses, in what villages or towns?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you earlier, it was in the Knin region around, but I can't remember the names of the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the agency or UN organization that passed this information?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I told you, we had for every visit there was discussions around with all the internationals because we exchanged information to each other. This is, of course, a way that United Nations bodies are working. It was very important for human rights people to know from the military part and from the police which are the security risks. So this was information that was given from one agency to another, so that we were, so to say, all on the same track and were aware of. Also, the European Union bodies were involved in the discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you have the name of any individual we could speak to, to try to verify where this information came from? Do you have any recollection?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could imagine that those who are -- were working at that time in the staff can verify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Who -- on your staff you mean?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And what are the names of the people who were working on your staff? I don't think we established that yet.

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a lot of them. Of course, Roman Wieruszewski was the head of all this. I have a very bad copy. Then we had Mamadi Diakite who has been mentioned earlier. One person that was very much involved in these who was local secretariat assistance was Mr. Sasa Milosevic, and then also Susan Ashoor who was local. Ravinder Joshi was there. Then from -- sometimes we had people coming from other parts of our mission in Bosnia, in Herzegovina, in Kosovo, in -- from Belgrade, and so on. So it was a good team of people who assisted each other. So there are some of the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Sasa Milosevic you mentioned. Sasa Milosevic on your team was from the Serbian Helsinki Committee; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not to my knowledge. He was working for us as a secretarial assistance local. He can be nowadays perhaps, I don't know. I haven't heard about him since I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could call up 1D40-0081.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This relates, Mrs. Rehn, to the portion of your 7 November 1995 report at paragraph 1. You refer to a couple thousand Croatian Serbs awaiting return from Hungary, and I believe you mentioned that yesterday in your testimony as well.

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a news article from 22nd of September, 1995, about this issue, and it says: "Croatian police has barred nine elderly Serbs from returning to their homes in Croatia's Krajina region, the Helsinki Commission for Human Rights said on Friday. The group was stopped at Terezino Polje north-eastern Croatia, on the border with Hungary, the committee said. But it was not immediately clear when the border incident happened." Then it goes on: "'We have sent letters to the Croatian government as well as the Croatian office for refugees about the group, but they have not replied,' said Petar Mrkalj, the director of the Croatian branch of the Helsinki committee, in a communique" Now, that was on the 22nd of September; and in your 7 November 1995 report where you discuss at paragraph 41 this issue about the Croatian Serbs being at the Hungarian border, in the appendix it reports that, on Thursday 12 October, you met with Petar Mrkalj, who's mentioned in this article. And my question to you is: At least as of 22nd September 1995, Mr. Mrkalj is telling agency France-Presse that the number of Serbs in Hungary that was turned away was nine. So I was wondering if you could tell us where the number of thousands of Serbs at the Hungarian border, where you had arrived at that number.

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is an information I have got from the leadership of my office and through also the Eastern Slavonia people working there. So I could imagine that the word at the border is not perhaps an accurate saying; but in Hungary, that they are waiting in Hungary. So there I must totally agree with you, counsel, that it was not exact. But the information I got then through, again, my staff was that people are waiting in Hungary and there are hundreds if even not thousands who are waiting to get their papers -- papers in order. And that was, of course, everything. Everything was in connection to the property rights, as I have told earlier. It was not so much a question of getting your nationality confirmed. You are totally right that it was in Belgrade, as I also told. You should go to Belgrade to get your IDs and others if possible. But the time-limit to get, to claim for your property --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn --

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that was short, and, therefore, it was so important to look into the situation that people are waiting somewhere to get to -- to get back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. But just so that we're clear now, what you're saying is you're not sure of how many people were in Hungary actually waiting to come --

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm quite sure that they were in Hungary. But at the border, that is certainly an exaggeration, because when you talk about the border, then you are just standing there at the check-point waiting to come. And there could have be nine; certainly, there are nine, as it is told here. But, in Hungary, altogether many were waiting for an entrance to come back again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Would again we have to speak with your staff to figure out where these numbers come from?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. And in everything -- almost everything that I haven't seen with my own eyes, you have to talk with my staff, because I have to remind you, once again, that this was a mission with the Special Rapporteur. Sometimes even Special Rapporteurs have never visited the country they are reporting on when they are not allowed to go there. But in my case, I really went there very often. But all the other information was gathered by the staff, then discussed by us, and I looked into it that it is safe information that you can put in a report. And as with the meaning of the report is to raise awareness with the governments, the different governments I covered. I think it was a very good way of a method. Even looking at now, if I still may say, that we achieved our purpose with a lot of answers, very good, very strong, very detailed answers, from the governments that led also to steps to be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Rehn. Please don't take this as being rude. I'm just --

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have seen more rude people in my time than you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you to, if you can, keep your answers a bit shorter, so that we can get all through --

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. That is my interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is what I was about to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender this exhibit into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D688, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D688 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, at page 4 of your statement, you refer to the Secretary-General's report from December 1995, and it says: "On page 5, the estimated figure of destroyed houses of 5.000 was an estimate obtained from the collected information from the international organizations including my own office. I witnessed myself many burned houses in the Krajina region." The number of 5.000 burned houses, that was both Sectors North and South; correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to that report which is P477, and if we could go to page 4 of that document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 14, here's what the Secretary-General reports. He says: "It is not possible to provide the exact number of houses destroyed by fire in former Sectors North and South; although, the estimated total is in excess of 5.000. Based on observations by teams patrolling throughout the Krajina, the ECMM estimates that in rural areas, 60 per cent of the homes in former Sector South and 30 per cent of the in former Sector North have been destroyed by fire. United Nations military observers visited 389 villages in Sector South and found that, out of 21.744 houses, 16.857 had been destroyed by fire or had sustained some damage; although, this figure includes damage from before 'Operation Storm.'" Now, both the Secretary-General and you in your statement use the figure of 5.000, rather than relying on the UNMO figure of 16.857. Is that because you were unable to determine from the numbers that been provided by UNMO which of those houses had been destroyed before and which after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is just the reason why we took this quite careful standpoint that not exaggerate in any case. It was very difficult altogether to make any kind of estimate on what was the actual amount of houses destroyed during Operation Storm. As you rightly just pointed out, that there were houses destroyed also earlier and burnt down, even if certainly forensic experts can tell when something has been burnt, is it today or several years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But you had -- when you were preparing your reports, you had access to the ECMM analysis of houses or structures destroyed by fire or that had sustained some damage before preparing your reports; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if I understood your testimony correctly, you didn't use those numbers because you didn't want to be exaggerating anything?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And as we didn't exactly know how much was a result of the Operation Storm and what had happened already earlier. I think that and I would remember that we decided in this international community to be -- to really take this amount of plus/minus 5.000 as at least showing that it was a lot of houses because 5.000 is really a big amount of destroyment. So I would say that was the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And looking at paragraph 14 of the Secretary-General's report, does that refresh your recollection, when you were having these conversations about using the 5.000 plus/minus number, that was intended to be a number combined for both Sectors North and South? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be lying if I said that I'm recalling this, but I could find it possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Staying with this report, if we could go to -- oh, sorry. It's the -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I need to take you back to the 7 November 1995 report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, have you dealt with these numbers because then I would have --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- an additional question. You said we didn't want to exaggerate. Now, we see a number of 5.000, we see a number of over 15.000. Was it that you considered the higher number to be an exaggerates, or did you want to give such conservative numbers so as to avoid a risk of exaggeration? Which of the two was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would rather say that it was the risk of exaggeration that we were afraid of, because we wanted to be very in one way modest with what we said. It gave a better base to also demand steps when there was not a risk of exaggeration. But I have to say that these figures, they are not putting any bells ringing in my mind, in my head, in my memory, because as you well know these reports are filled with details and it's some time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's understood. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to P639, please, and if we could go to page 6 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Rehn, at paragraph 11, you talk about "the temporary suspension of the constitutional law on human rights and freedoms and the rights of national and ethnic minorities -- communities or minorities in the Republic of Croatia ..." Towards the middle, it says: "The decision to suspend articles which guarantee the special status of districts predominantly populated by national minorities, create separate educational institutions, and secure proportional representation in the parliament, government, and judiciary, places a question mark over the attitude of the Croatian authorities towards national minorities in general and the Serbian minority in particular." And then at paragraph 12: "The Special Rapporteur also notes with concern that Article 60 of the above-mentioned law establishing the Provisional Human Rights Court has been suspended." Now -- and back to paragraph 11, there's a sentence in there that says -- referring now to the constitutional law on human rights, it says: "Although that law was never fully implemented, it nevertheless provided national minorities with important legal guarantees." My first question to you was: Did the phrase "never fully implemented," do you recall whether any portion of that law was ever implemented?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that under the law, there were supposed to be special districts created essentially in what were former Sectors North and Sectors South for the ethnic Serb community?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible; but as I said, I can't recall exactly what was meant to be in this law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall in your conversations with your interlocutors in the Croatian government that them ever telling you or writing to you that the law couldn't be implemented after Operation Storm because the Serbian population had left?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- I have copies, I believe, of all the letters written to me, and it was not mentioned in these letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that under that law, all institutions at the local level and at the -- what was referred to as the Kotar level or the administration level, the police departments, they all had to reflect an ethnic composition equal to the ethnic composition of the area in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really hope that it was meant to be so. I myself am a representative of a minority in my own country, and I know exactly how important it is to have the rights for minorities written into the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, speaking of this specific allow, though, are you aware -- I'll give you an example just to provide you with the numbers. If a particular town had 70 per cent Serbs and 30 per cent Croats, are you aware that this law required that seven police officers in the police station had to be Serb and three police officers had to be Croats?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That is very much in line with other laws regarding minorities, including my own country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And teachers in schools, if there were 70 per cent Serbs, it required seven out of every ten teachers in the schools had to be Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand what you are looking to, when the Serbs left, it was not actual to implement this law. On the other hand, to postpone it meant too that they didn't count on the Serb citizens to be quickly back again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, may I ask a question. May I go back to the previous question. Mr. Misetic asked you whether you were aware that this was a component of that law.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your answer said, more or less at least as I understood it, that that would be logical because it would reflect what we find elsewhere as well. The question, however, was whether you knew that this law contained these kind of provisions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Because we discussed it, of course, that it was a question of getting the balance between the majorities and minorities in the official bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you were aware --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of these provisions to be part of that legislation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that even in that short-term period, as the security situation in Sectors North and South was poor, that this law provided an additional complicating factor and that by law all the institutions had to be set up with Serbs participating at all levels of government in those areas? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And, therefore, too we are not strong in our wordings. We are noting with concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to your reference to Article 60 of the law which establishes a provisional human rights court, are you aware that such a court never came into existence?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And are you aware that the reason it never came into existence is that, in the law itself, it requires an international agreement between the republics of the former Yugoslavia to be established?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I certainly was aware of this then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me, this part of the rights were very strongly focused on the Ombudsman office, and that I was very pleased that could be established, as I told you yesterday, very much on my insistence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And you will recall, and I think there's -- it's in some of the documents that have been tendered through the Prosecution, that Croatia told you that it was not going to establish a separate provisional human rights court because Croatia was about to accede to the council of Europe and was, therefore, of the opinion that the European Court of Human Rights was itself a human right's court that would have jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And as I told the Court, therefore we expressed ourselves with concern and that was something we were concerned about, because at that time we didn't know when the report was made what will be the development of this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 14 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At paragraph 37 at the bottom, you discuss where you: " ... the Special Rapporteur held discussions with the Croatian authorities concerning the recently adopted law on the temporary take-over and management of certain property. This law allows the Croatian authorities to assume control over 'abandoned property' which may then be given to Croatian displaced persons and refugees for 'temporary possession and use.'" The last sentence then says: "The Special Rapporteur was informed by the Croatian authorities that the purpose of the new law was to protect abandoned property and to secure it for the possible return of the legitimate owners."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At paragraph 38, there's a brief legal analysis of Croatian law, and the second-to-last sentence says: "However, the law on the temporary take-over and management of certain property constitutes a de facto confiscation." Do you recall the basis of your conclusion that that law amounts to a de facto confiscation?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's strongly based on my own experiences when talking to people around, especially in Sector South around Knin, because those who have tried to return and were already there, the Serbs, they had already their houses occupied. I understand quite well that Croatian government had a lot of problems with those who had escaped from Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croats, that should be settled somewhere. They had a big population of refugees. But what was absolutely unacceptable was that there were cases where Croatians, who had their home, their house, apartment, for instance, in Zagreb, could get as a second house one of those left by Serbs. And that was something that I experienced personally, talked to them; and I have to say that I was not met very nicely by the people who were occupying the houses. And I think this was something that was unacceptable. If they would have been compensated for their property, then it could have been some kind of deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So talking right to that issue of compensation, do you know -- would you agree with me that a confiscation is a legal seizure without compensation by the government republican authority? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A confiscation, yes; but we thought that there were not grounds for confiscation, and that it should have been -- perhaps, as I have said earlier, I'm not a lawyer and I have difficulties with all these legal expressions because you should have studied law to be able to work out the right words for everything. But what we were really concerned about was that people couldn't move into their houses, somebody else was living there, and they didn't have any hope of coming there without getting a compensation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You use the phrase de facto confiscation. By using the phrase de facto confiscation, did you mean that it wasn't a de jure confiscation?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know the difference between sequestration or sequester and confiscation?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could call up 65 ter 2502, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, this is a legal analysis of that law which may have been sent to you in anticipation of the report that you were preparing. Sasa Milosevic ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page of that document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: ... whom you had referenced earlier is on the e-mail as the person at the top. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And it's being forwarded -- this purports to be a legal analysis of the Croatian property law. The cover page said it was forwarded to the -- actually, Mr. Wieruszewski. It was to his attention, but also Mr. Mautner Markhof, on 23 October 1995. If you look at the header, it's an e-mail, 6 October 1995, forwarded to Sasa Milosevic of your staff, from the -- what appears to be the Helsinki Committee in Belgrade. Do you see that? Do you recall if the legal analysis in your report is based on a legal analysis that had been drafted in Belgrade by the Serbian Helsinki Committee, passed to Sasa Milosevic, and then passed to Mr. Wieruszewski in anticipation of your report?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no memory of this paper. I wonder if I ever have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender this document in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the first thing is we haven't got notice that this document was going to be tendered, and, therefore, I haven't been able to look at this document. May I just have a moment. Can this be taken up later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's a 65 ter, Your Honour, but I assume they were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, a 65 ter as such doesn't mean you are going to use that as evidence, and I think the rule is that at the beginning of the cross-examination, you inform the other party what they could expect as far as documents to be used during cross-examination. So familiarity with the document as such can be assumed, but awareness of it being used at this moment cannot be assumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I apologise. I think it was just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, apart from that, the top seven lines --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually, I'm looking at the e-court report and it was disclosed to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, if that's the case, we lost one minute for no good purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's number 14 in the e-court list.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have objection to the admission. I've taken the time to quickly go through it, and I apologise if I delayed the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Mr. Misetic, the copy or the scanned version, but perhaps I should address Ms. Mahindaratne, leaves out a bit of the left margin, and since we find Sasa Milosevic once as "2" or perhaps the original "2," and a few lines further down origin Sasa Milosevic, so he could have forwarded it. Could we have a complete copy of this document, so that we're better able to understand what at least the document tells us, where it comes from, and where it was sent to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, during the break, I will look at this and take care of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I think we should marked for identification for the time being. It's on the record. There are no objections against admission, but the Chamber would like to see the document from left to right. It further indicates, Ms. Mahindaratne, that this is the second page out of eight. I don't know what series it is in, and I don't know whether this's any relevance in the remaining seven pages. Mr. Registrar, this would be number ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit Number D689, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, now we turn to page 4 of your statement. In the second paragraph, again you're referring to the Secretary-General's report, I believe, yes, of 18 October 1995. And you note that: "It is mentioned that the Croatian authorities have warned that against the return of the Serbs to their homes in the Krajina because of an uncertain security situation and have said that a mass return must await a final political settlement." Now, in October, you had conversations with UNHCR as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is that a yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Rehn --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the record, we request you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was so deeply involved with the text that I was only nodding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not a criticism. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, you are aware that the High Commissioner for Refugees was Sadako Ogata at that time?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. We had a lot of good cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of what Mrs. Ogata's position was in October of 1995 with respect to mass returns?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I just can't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have 1D40-0054, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And at the top, you will see that is a statement by Mrs. Ogata, 10 October 1995, given to the Humanitarian Issues Working Group of the International Conference for the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 3 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At the bottom paragraph, it says: "Allow me now to elaborate on the issues of peace and the return of refugees." Then there's an introduction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The second paragraph -- the first full paragraph says: "In order to carry out the return operation, I must emphasize the importance of having internationally recognised humanitarian principles. First of all, it must be voluntary. People must not be used as pawns. The interest of every individual refugee should be the motivating force behind any repatriation process and not political considerations." The next paragraph says: "Secondly, repatriation must take place in an organized, phased manner. If it is to take place in dignity, attention must be paid to ensuring that, for example, adequate accommodation and basic essential services are available in the places of return. " Then the next paragraph: "I envisage the repatriation process broadly taking place in three phases. The first should be the return of displaced persons within Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia. During this initial post-settlement period, there are also likely to be further population movements as a result of the territorial adjustments between the parties." Does that refresh your recollection as to what was being discussed in these working groups on the former Yugoslavia and what Mrs. Ogata may have been discussing with respect to the process of how refugees were to return?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is definitely no kind of contradiction between her policy and what I have been reported on -- reporting on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not --

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something that I find very important to mention is that the returns, the voluntariness is really very important. But I met with Serb refugees outside Belgrade in quite terrible camps, and they definitely wanted to return. So as always, my reports are based on the ordinary, real people, not how to move them like just something you are playing games with. I'm not saying that Mrs. Ogata is doing that. But, though, it was very important that whatever I reported on was coming out from the feelings of the real grass-root level, not high politicians, not even international organizations. Then I also have again to remind that a Special Rapporteur is totally independent from the United Nations organizations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I -- you should never assume that I'm putting something to you because I think it's in contradiction to what you've said. What I'm asking about is the Croatian government's position as articulated in your own witness statement.

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And, here, it's very good where Madam is Ogata especially mentioning this, that this must be voluntary and security must be guaranteed. And that is what the Croatian authorities were not prepared to give that guarantee at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What guarantee?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of security at that time for the returnees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Because the security situation still had not been --

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And especially because the Croatians there didn't want them to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well --

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The neighbours didn't want them to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The neighbours, okay. Now, what I'm asking you is on the issue of the Croatian government saying that mass returns needed to await a political settlement and for an improved security situation. That was consistent with what UNHCR was putting forward at working groups on the former Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the way that as they couldn't provide and perhaps didn't want to provide a strong security situation for the returnees. Just because of that, of course they didn't want to go against their own people, Croatian people who lived there, and didn't want them to come back. This is very much a political settlement, as you said. They didn't want to settle it. I know politicians so well, I have been myself one. So I know they are looking into what the people, the voters, really want you to do. And in this case, their own people, Croatian people who was there in the villages, in town of Knin and so on, they didn't want them to come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, I think we went through this yesterday, but after the political settlement was achieved, by the time you filed your last report you said that there was reason for optimism in light of what the Croatian government had done after the political settlement was achieved; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, several years or a couple of years later on. And today of course they will be a member of the European Union soon, a fantastic development.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender this document from the UNHCR into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D690, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D690 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Misetic, when Mrs. Rehn said the government and the neighbours, before putting your next question, question, you said "the neighbours," which as a matter of fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, I will not at the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the transcript doesn't reflect that. It says "the," and then the word "neighbours" is left out. You repeated that word and that's part an answer, and that's not how it should be done. If you look at -- it's just that it was missing on the transcript. The word "the" is there, but the word "neighbours" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think we're referring to page 28, line 17, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you look at page 28, line 18, it now reads "the, okay."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There you said "the neighbours."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's good it's not on the record because repeating the part of the answer which apparently is most welcome is not -- comes down to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You inserted the word "Croatian government," and that is not in the transcript, which is why I'm looking it up. She said "the Croatians ..." --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "The Croatians."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's why I wanted to clarify, so that later on we wouldn't have the misunderstanding, or I wanted to clarify what "Croatians" meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, a few lines before it's "Croatian authorities," and it's a clear reference to that, even if the word "authorities" was not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, again, I mean, I don't think that's what -- it says: "The Croatian authorities were not prepared to give that guarantee of security," and then she added: "... and especially because the Croatians there didn't want them to come."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you asked: "What guarantee?" Then the answer was: "... of security at the time for the returnees." That is clearly a reference to the earlier line about guarantee, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I distinguish, Your Honour, between being able to provide a security guarantee and not wanting somebody -- but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's leave it. If perhaps by not repeating the answer at all, we avoid these kind of risks, or you asked what did you mean by this or that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, I noted in your curriculum vitae that you were also the chair of the democratization and human rights working table from 2004 to 2005 for the stability pact for south-east Europe; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As the chair of the democratization and human rights working table, would that mean that you were involved in human rights issues throughout the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The south-eastern Europe, so Albania and Moldova and others, were included in this. So the stability pact for south-eastern Europe was created in 1998 in Sarajevo, and there were three working tables, one for democracy and so on. So then I covered the whole region of south-eastern Europe; also Croatia, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: All right. And this was in 2004?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I started 2003 and left it in the beginning of 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me call up 1D40-0059.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You will note on the cover page that this is a meeting of the Security Council on the 5th of September, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In the right-hand column three paragraphs down, it says: "At the meeting, the Security Council will hear a briefing by Mr. Hedi Annabi, assistant Secretary-General for peacekeeping operations. "I now give the floor to Mr. Annabi."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 5, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The third full paragraph down, this is Mr. Annabi's presentation to the Security Council, and he says -- now we're talking about mass returns of refugees to Kosovo. He says: "In this context, recent statements by Kosovo Serb internally displaced persons that they are planning to block the crossing points on the administrative boundary line with Kosovo later this month if they are not allowed to return en masse are cause for concern. Although the impatience of internally displaced persons is understandable, given the still delicate state of inter-communal relations, any action along those lines would only be counterproductive and would be harmful to the returns process. "There cannot be artificial mass return. UNMIK's return policy is based on the right of individual return in an organized way so that it can be sustainable. This requires careful preparation on the ground to ensure that the physical infrastructure - meaning houses, employment, and access to public services - is in place to welcome the returnees. It also requires a careful handling of relations with the neighbouring Kosovo Albanian communities to diminish the potential for return-related security incidents." Now, as someone who not only covered Croatia but covered the former Yugoslavia and later became involved even after this report in human rights in the former Yugoslavia, you are aware that there was a specific structured return policy to bring Serbs back into Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- and that the United Nations itself was opposed to a policy of mass return of Serbs to Kosovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we are going quite far now from the situation with my reports when we talk about the returns of Serbs to Kosovo. Because what I at least have learned studying conflicts in and around the world with another -- other mission I had for UN, that one conflict is not similar to another. And I have good respect for my old friend Mr. Steiner, but we could, of course, refer to whichever presentation from important persons. So this was a matter that certainly was very important, found important, regarding Kosovo after the intervention and the bombings and all these what happened there. But I can't see that there should be any kind of contradiction to, because I haven't been asking for mass returns myself. I have been asking for security and to have voluntary returns. If there are many of them, then it's okay. So I think that we have the same principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My question again was: Were you aware as you were working on the stability pact of the United Nations policy on mass return --

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I was aware. I started -- this was 2002, yes, I started in the end of 2003, and there were new guys who were in the leadership of Kosovo mission UNMIK then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender this Security Council document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit Number D691, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D691 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will finish by the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to, because of your knowledge of the events of the situation in Kosovo, call up 1D40-0484. Mrs. Rehn, this is an OSCE report from December of 1999. It is titled: "As Seen, As Told, part II." It is an OSCE analysis of what happened between June and October of 1999 in Kosovo after the United Nations and NATO entered Kosovo. I'm going to read you a few portions of the foreword.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The document itself is almost 400 pages so we have not uploaded the entire document into evidence; although, it's available if the Court and the Prosecution wish. If we could turn to page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Although it's an OSCE report, the special representative of the UN Secretary-General, Dr. Bernard Kouchner, prepared the foreword. He was the Secretary-General's representative to Kosovo during this time-period. And if you note at the beginning, Mr. Kouchner says: "This report makes sobering reading. The human rights violations detailed by the OSCE's Human Rights Division for the period June-October 1999 include executions, abductions, torture, cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatment, arbitrary arrests, and attempts to restrict freedom of expression." The last sentence in that paragraph says: "Such extensive violations of fundamental human rights challenge everyone here and the United Nations interim administration in Kosovo, who are striving to create the rule of law and respect for human rights, to do more to address the root causes of abuses." The bottom paragraph on that page: "In many of the cases documented by the OSCE in this report, there are serious indications that the perpetrators of human rights violations are either members of the former UCK, people passing themselves off as members of the former UCK, or members of other armed Albanian groups." Then it goes on: "In many cases, it has been so far impossible to identify exactly those responsible."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kouchner in the first full paragraph, second or third sentence says: "We in UNMIK are taking concrete, practical steps to prevent violations. Nevertheless, the United Nations international civilian police and KFOR need to increase their already impressive activities in Kosovo. Frequent and visible patrols and developing closer ties to the community will help prevent violations and increase the likelihood of arresting those suspected of committing human rights violations."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Then, finally, two pages up, not the next page but the page after.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The top of the page, it says: "The legacy of human rights violations that occurred before, during, and after the conflict is a heavy one. Recovering from a war is difficult enough, but the problems are multiplied when the roots of the conflict are essentially a massive and systematic disregard for human rights. This report underscores just how difficult the task is. Vengeance and fear are all too common in post-conflict Kosovo. This vengeance and fear has led to ongoing human rights violations." And then third paragraph: "We are deeply concerned about the situation of minorities. A close look at the trend in crime shows a clear improvement. A drop from 50 murders during each of the first weeks to three murders last week cannot be ignored." Now, I'm stop there. Dr. Kouchner in Kosovo six months after the UN entered Kosovo says: "A drop from 50 murders during each of the first weeks to three murders last week cannot be ignored." Are you aware in Croatia of what the murder rate was in Sector South in August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not just without having any kind of statistics here in front of me; and, here again, I have to say with that all situations are very different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me --

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll continue on here and then we can wrap up because I only have --

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this jump to Kosovo, very, very familiar to me, is a little bit I wouldn't say disturbing but surprising perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's continue on, Mrs. Rehn. It goes on to say: "It is not fair to make comparisons with the situation before or during the war. At that time, and for at least a decade, there was a systematic policy of apartheid, a sub-human status, or at least a sub-community status for Albanians in Kosovo. This is no longer the case today. Perhaps it may seem just as bad today for the Serbs or Roma who live in fear, who cannot move about freely or have to find a way to protect their children, but it is no longer a matter of a policy. All the parties in Kosovo, all leaders, Serbs and Albanians, have stated their positions in favour of a multi-ethnic society and co-existence among all communities. "The crimes we see are the acts of individuals. No political party has claimed responsibility for them. Their representatives in the Kosovo Transitional Council have condemned these abuses every time, and they themselves have expressed their concern over the acts of intolerance. We cannot exclude the possibility of double talk, but we cannot presuppose it either." Let me wrap up by asking you this: Dr. Kouchner talks about how the leaders talked about wanting a multi-ethnic society and co-existence among all communities; and at the beginning of my cross-examination, we played a tape of what President Tudjman had said to you on 4 December 1995. Do you agree with me then that what President Tudjman was discussing there was reconciliation between Serbs and Croats; correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that it is of course, as Dr. Kouchner here phrased it, it was possible that he was engaged in double talk and that possibility can't be excluded but we shouldn't presuppose it either? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. It's very similar to what I felt about my discussions with President Tudjman and members of the Government of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Rehn. Thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President. May I just request the Defence to upload the cover page of the document so that we have a complete document available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, quite frankly, when I downloaded this years ago, it didn't have a cover page, and now the OSCE site was down when I tried to find it this weekend. Certainly, I will try to find it. It's on the internet or should be anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That for the time is not an objection against admission, then?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this becomes D692.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Rehn, Mr. Misetic stopped you when you expressed your surprise about the comparison made. If you would like to add anything to that, you're free to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was -- is this working? Yes, this is working. I was a little bit surprised because, as I said, before every situation, every conflict unfortunately has similarities with the suffering of civilians nowadays, but also they are quite different. And when Mr. Kouchner, or should we call him Minister Kouchner now, was the first SIG to take over at UNMIK, he had his talks and that was quite obvious that he was upset about the situation and also heard all these quite nice words from all the different parties. Of course, if we should take a letter from today, so many years later, that could be another tone in these. But there are so many different situations. I'm only surprised that justice with Kosovo will be brought -- brought to this trial. I could have many, many, many own reports on the situation there now and earlier and so, but it's not the case for this trial. I only wanted to express my surprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a break, but not until after I have formally admitted into evidence D692. We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, during the break, I did take a look at the e-mail that we -- that the Defence moved to tender, and it is, in fact, an eight-page document containing seven pages of e-mail. I have no objections to its admission; however, we downloaded the document from the system and it seems that the margin on the system itself is not there. But we are now examining the original in the Word to ensure that we could get a better copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the parties could agree on who sent it and when and to whom, then, of course, that would certainly assist. It's a bit of analysis of the header which is a rather complicated one because it has been forwarded apparently to another receiver.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's another point, Mr. President. I wasn't clear based on the e-mail addresses as to whether, in fact, it was an e-mail going from Helsinki Belgrade, but perhaps Mr. Misetic might indicate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's an e-mail, but a copy of this e-mail apparently was sent by Telefax, because we also find the fax header 26th of October, if I remember well. So let's try to analyse what or how the communications went at the time, and then we can further focus on the content. I'd like to hear from the parties whether there's any agreement on this. Looking at my right, no one is yet standing, but, Mr. Kay, you'll be the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Kay, who's counsel for Mr. Cermak. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, what we're going to look at is some documents which is a snap-shot of measures taken by relevant Croatian government ministries in relation to trying to stop crimes, and this is relevant to one of your reports filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And for reference purposes, it doesn't need to be brought up, but so it can be considered by Their Honours, Exhibit P639, page 11, paragraph 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The first document I'd like you to look at is already in evidence, D49. This is a document that is dated the 18th of August, 1995, it comes from the assistant minister of the Ministry of the Interior, and it was sent by that minister whose name is Josko Maric. First of all, did you ever meet Josko Moric?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible but I can't recall it. I told you and told the Court earlier that I'm very bad with names; and perhaps if I see his face, that's quite something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I quite understand. This was sent by him. He worked in the Ministry of the Interior, the MUP, to the police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we turn to page 2 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The Court are familiar with this document, Mrs. Rehn. And on page 2 of the document, you can see in the text there that he has received information about torching of houses, taking away property, and he refers to most of the acts being perpetrated by individuals wearing Croatian army uniforms. Then he deals there in the text with whether they are or are not members of the Croatian army. He says, as you can see, that these acts are inflicting political damage on the Republic of Croatia, and then he makes an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we turn to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In this order, he tells the police administration chiefs. Again, the Court are familiar with the structure within the Croatian law of police stations and administration chiefs. Were you familiar with the internal structure of the Croatian system of policing?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, we talked about it, and it was presented to me when I was there. This letter, of course, was written before my mandate started, 18th of August; but, of course, we talked about how the structures were built up within the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. We're going to look at a series of documents now going from August to September. Don't worry about the date. It's the orders that are relevant. Of course, when you're writing your reports, these are already in order. You can see that there is an order to convene a meeting with the military police. Paragraph 2 deals with the torching of houses, taking of property, not to be operatively investigated in the sense of those that have hitherto occurred, but a stop must be put to cases of this type as of today. Paragraph 3 deals with military police and check-points, mixed patrols of civilian and military police to be set up. And in paragraph 4, on-site investigations, forensic, and operative processing will be conducted after every case. Paragraph 5, if the military police cannot perform the task mentioned in 4, the civilian police will do it alone irrespective of whether the perpetrator wears an army uniform or not. Next page, page 4, deals with the dissemination of this particular order. And in your report that I've just referred to, you were told by the Croatian higher authorities that they had taken steps and measures in relation to trying to prevent crime; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at the next document. As I said, it's a snap-shot of seven, just to put the picture to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is D584 as marked for identification, Exhibit D584. It is dated the 19th of August, 1995, otherwise called 65 ter 4595, if that makes it easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we'll be looking at a document dated the 19th of August from one of those police administrations back to the MUP and the assistant minister, Mr. Moric. And it refers to the document we've just looked at. And in this document which is sent by a chief of the Zadar-Knin police administration, he refers to a meeting between the military police and the police administration of Zadar-Knin. But we can note that the military police pointed out that coordinated action at all check-points was impossible due to lack of personnel. And page 2 of this document is just a conclusion. We don't need to go into that document. Were you informed about the coordination between the military police and the local police?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, but I'm not sure about this. This is interesting, though, with the dates that they had taken steps and had meetings already before they got the letter from MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And these are -- this is relevant to matters you were discussing with the government, of course. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we go to the next document, which is D50.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 22nd of August. Again, it's from the MUP. It's from Mr. Moric, the assistant minister, again to the police stations. Again, it refers to the telegram of the 18th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we turn to page 2, we get to the substance of the text.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if perhaps it could be read, it doesn't say "police stations" but "police administrations," just so we have the terminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 2 is the text. Have a look at that text there to do with the issue of the burning of houses, taking of property unlawfully. The letter was sent by Mr. Moric to the military police describing the magnitude and significance of the issue. Military police administration sending an order to the military police battalions, telling them to link with the MUP and police stations to solve the problem, and then requiring monitoring and information about the level of cooperations between the police and the military police. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And a series of questions looking at relevant matters to see how effective these tasks were being performed. Do you note that?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And would you agree this kind of step and measure is the sort of matter that you would have approved of at the time?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. And all these measures asked for are exactly what we would have -- we would have wanted also to happen concretely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And we can turn to the next page, page 3, where information about investigations as well is required. And I take it your answer would be the same as you've just given, that this would be important from your perspective; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Did anyone inform you on your team about these particular measures when you came in on the 27th of September?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite possible, but I can't confirm it because coming for the first time to the region in war, I had been -- oh, yes, I was a minister of defence, but that's something else, and not on the same good level as these with the realities. And I'm sure that I was told about what was asked for also was repeated in my meetings with authorities. Of course, these detailed letters I didn't have access to, I'm quite sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it is fair to say that in your reports to the Secretary-General, that this kind of detail is not in those reports that you have filed?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They are not in the sense that, of course, we are telling about the wishes and also the intentions of the authorities. But we -- of course, we've heard a lot what we saw in practice out in the villages, and that these orders were not in any case fully followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next document is under seal, Your Honours, and measures have to be taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- a matter not just to be shown to the public or would the testimony also be confidential?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The testimony won't be confidential because that can be dealt with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the next document should not be shown to the public and that would be, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document here that you can see on the screen, Mrs. Rehn. I'm not going to go into the detail. You understand it's a document that's under seal. You understand why I'm doing this, do you?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if I get it. Now it's here in English. It was not in the beginning. Let's see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There's no need to go into some of the detail, but you can see here that the matters of check-points, coordination, patrols are dealt with.

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And issues of cooperation, all measures that I'm sure you would approve of; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We can move on from there as we don't need to spend longer with it, and I know the Trial Chamber are familiar with the evidence. Let us turn now to the next document, D589, as it has been MFI'd. It is 65 ter 1302. It's not under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's dated the 28th of August, it's from the Zadar-Knin police administration sent to that assistant minister, Mr. Moric, who's been involved with this series of orders from the MUP, and it concerns the treatment of people in military uniforms in the liberated area and refers to a significant number of persons wearing Croatian army uniforms, carrying weapons, driving vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It refers to such people at the top of the page probably being in concert with relatives, friends, and the like, taking property, driving it away, on the basis of written corroborations issued by municipal presidents. So, obviously, some sort of fraud going on with people with false papers. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
