utterances.text: Would you accept that the situation faced by the Government of Croatia at this time dealing with these liberated territories posed upon them very difficult administrative problems to enforce and maintain the rule of law?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, it was tricky for them to find out who was really military and when they were wearing uniform, something that I have already also made clear in my earlier statements here today and yesterday. A post-conflict time is always difficult to administer, but, of course, you should do your best in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And it depends upon the level of resources of a particular government. It goes without saying, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Further down the page the author thought it necessary, deemed it necessary, that the local police or persons authorised them should be present at meetings that General Cermak held with members of UNCRO, UNCIVPOL, and other international organizations to ensure police are informed about all agreements. Page 3, it's only two lines but it's always unsatisfactory not finishing a sentence. Inform them of conclusions reached which will enable them to organize and plan tasks and duties from their purview accordingly. Again, measures, I'm sure you would agree, whereby the Croatian ministry is trying to deal with the problems that they were faced?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, they were trying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we've only got two more documents, P499, which is under seal. Again, we can look at this document without going into any substantive information, Your Honour, so I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not to be shown on the screen, but no need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We can all look at this document. I think you've probably got the hang of it now, Mrs. Rehn; would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soon, not now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I mean about me not going into the detail.

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's dated the 1st of September. And as the text comes up on the screen, you can see that there are problems with the military police. If we turn to page 2, those problems are identified and you see the wearing of Croatian army uniforms and units that are mopping-up the area from isolated paramilitary units. That's all we need to go into. Again, this would have been a document that you probably wouldn't have seen; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You agree that it shows a sort of continuum of orders that were being issued at the ministry level?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely, as the -- as the actions are still going on all the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- even if there are other orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There are others. I've taken a little snap-shot to show you on this matter without taking up too much court time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The last document is a public document, D596. I'm told to use the 2D numbers. This is another MFI, 2D04-0216. The translation is 18. Yes. I'm getting the hang of reading the documents in B/C/S now. This is a document dated the 19th of September to the police administrations. You can see Zadar-Knin, Knin there, referring to an earlier telegram which the Court is familiar with, referring to the fact that on the 15th of September, the military police is no longer present at entrance and exit check-points to the liberated areas. Activities of the military police will include car patrols assigned to the task of constant patrolling, obligatory reporting to "our," which would be the MUP, check-points and radio communications. Turning to page 2, the same assistant minister who signed this letter, Mr. Moric, has said: "Keep previous check-points, thus, that you change the locations of their establishment ..." And in essence what means, because people find ways of getting round check-points, move them around and more patrols and foot patrols to carry out basic police tasks. Last of the documents, but again the sort of information and actions that would have been in accordance with your wishes?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be very odd if I should say they are not because this is all what we wanted to happen also in the practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. We've looked actually at documents that range from the highest levels going down to a more basic level. So it's been all the way through in this snap-shot of documents throughout the system, so down to the police stations in the field not just being sent between ministry departments. Did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was there any presentation to you of these measures during your meetings?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the meetings with the ministers, I can't recall that they should have gone to practical details like these, very important details. It would have been gone if they could have been much more explicit with what they told, because they said we are doing everything we can and we are giving our orders to the police stations and so on and so on. Everybody's aware of what they should do, but, of course, the presentation of direct, and I think most of these letters are also strongly confidential. So they certainly didn't want to show anything like that, even if it would have been in their own interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The Court knows the evidence. This is part of, let me just say, a hundred documents, all right, this snap-shot, or more. It would have been helpful to you at the time to perhaps have a presentation, not necessarily by me but someone else, of what was happening in the system so that you could have reported on it, I dare say. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I reported that we got our overviews what was told to us from the ministerial level. But for us, of course, the most important thing was the orders were strictly also followed, that there was a clear tendency that every policeman or woman - I can't remember if there were police women then - that everyone really followed the orders in spite of the pressure perhaps from their fellow Croatians in the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You referred earlier this morning to the neighbours problem --

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- which you would agree is difficult to deal with?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. And I have many times stated that police are also human beings with all the weaknesses and the strength, and these are difficult things to be dealing with in your close neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. If you would allow me one second. Mr. Kuzmanovic, are you ready? Mrs. Rehn, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Kuzmanovic, who is counsel for Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to be covering a lot of documents with you, so we're going to need to have just a little bit of patience as they're called up. So I just want you to keep that in mind when I'm asking you questions and when you're giving me answers. Before I get into some of the documents, I wanted to follow-up on a few things that were discussed in your earlier testimony. You had mentioned that at one of your visits to Croatia, you personally had observed some looting that was going on; correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Who was with -- who was with your party when you observed this?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my first visit, that was in Sector North and I understood that I should not talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And then during my next visit, I had with me Roman Wieruszewski; I had with me my security officer, Heljo Laukkala, a major then in the Finnish army; and then we had an interpreter; and I can't recall who was then the interpreters for every of these. Somebody was also driving. It could have been Sasa Milosevic, it could have been somebody else. But we had always a team of the human rights staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you report this, what you observed, to any local police station or any local authorities that could have probably investigated it?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not directly, I didn't report, because it had -- it was also the duty of the staff to report on this. But, of course, I mentioned it in my meetings with the administration of -- on the ministerial level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So when you observed this as you were making your tour of Croatia, it's true, in fact, that at least at the time this occurred, you did not report this to any political or police authority while you were on your tour; correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met police officers during my visits. I always had meetings with police, and then I told about this. But I can't just make now a list of that. I have reported then, and then on that and that. Of course, we had a list then of everything that we saw that was made afterwards, and then brought to the attention of the Croatian authorities on different levels. But again, I have to recall that my work was -- I was living in Finland; I made my tours that the Human Rights Commission paid for the travel, DSA; and then I went back again to Finland. So that in that sense I was not there to take actions. I was a reporter, reporting on what I had seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Before you came to testify here in The Hague, did you meet with or talk with anyone other than representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor about your testimony here?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, when I was called for the first time in 2005, I talked with my security officer, who is now in a private company as chief of security, and so we talked about this and compared our impressions from those times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Who was that person?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Heljo Laukkala. His name is here in the papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: With my family of course, my children and grandchildren, not with my great-grandchild because she was too small.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: There was a discussion that you had during Mr. Misetic's cross-examination about the issue of what went on in Kosovo. I just wanted to ask you one question about that. The report that was read to you or the portion of the report that was read to you discussed that the murder rate had dropped from 50 murders per week to roughly three murders per week in a six-month time-frame. Were you aware that in that time-frame, the responsible authorities for maintaining law and order in Kosovo were UNMIK and KFOR?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, because I gave the report, the advices from when being the SIG for UNMIK to Secretary-General, some advices how the UNMIK should be built up from my experiences. So I was very strongly aware of what happened in Kosovo after all my years of reporting on Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And you were aware, were you not, that UNMIK and KFOR were very well equipped, very well trained, had the latest in technology available to them at that time?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, because I visited the Finnish contingent several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You had discussed during your direct examination your impressions about whether or not President Tudjman was interested in the plight of the Serb return to Croatia, and you thought or it was your impression you said that he was not interested in that. I wanted to ask you a question about that. Whether or not President Tudjman, as you say, was interested or not interested in the Serb return to Croatia, they did, in fact, return. At least as of January of 2000, a total of 41.000 Serbs returned to Croatia, did they not?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think what happened in 1995 in discussions is something that can't be compared with what happened until then 2000, because these times when I was reporting there was not a clear willingness of having the Serbs to return. So I think that we have all to be very grateful that perhaps partly, for a little part, my reports on the situation after Operation Storm in Croatia were helpful for the authorities to really take strong actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure, I understand you. I understand --

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because, of course, there must have been returns until 2000, and that has nothing to do with what was the atmosphere in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So at least you would agree that whether President Tudjman was or wasn't interested in their return, they did, in fact, return, and up to 41.000 returned as of January of 2000?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, out of 180.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many have returned to date?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea because my work is now in totally different parts of the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Would it surprise you to know that over 120.000 Serbs have returned to Croatia since 1995?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very pleased to have this figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to go through some documents with you now, please. Obviously, you wrote several reports during --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may ask counsel what the source of that -- the basis of that question was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we can look at D420, that was the source. It was admitted during Mr. Galbraith's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We don't have to put it up on the screen, but that's the source.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: There was a lot of discussion, Ms. Rehn, about things like amnesty for people who were involved in armed conflict against Croatia. You remember that discussion, do you not?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You were aware that from October of 1996 through June of 1998, there were close to 19.000 people who were amnestied by President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that figure. You have to remember that I also left my duties as Special Rapporteur in the end of 1997 when I entered as the SIG in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Were you aware of laws or decrees that were passed by President Tudjman amnestying people before Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of all these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, to save time and not deal with these documents directly with Ms. Rehn, since it's on this theme, we're preparing a bar table submission relating to amnesty and the number of people that were amnestied because it's on this topic. It's a lot of documentation that is taking a while to translate, but I just wanted to make the Court aware of that, that we will submit a bar table submission and obviously discuss it with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, of course, we would hear from the Prosecution if there's any objection against that. I noticed that quite a lot of time was spent on the amnesty issue here; whereas, my understanding of Mrs. Rehn's testimony is that, of course, it was very welcome to Serbs who wanted to return and were fearing that they might be investigated and prosecuted for having been a member of the armed forces of the ARSK or the ARSK, that that was one concern; but that there was another concern that those who were not amnestied and were suspected of having committed war crimes, whether Serbs or Croats, that that would happen. And I noticed that quite a lot of the attention was shifted from what I understood one apparent concern of Mrs. Rehn, that is, no investigations, no prosecutions against Croats suspected of having committed war crimes, that that was a concern which was a bit different from whether the matter that Serbs were fearing to be prosecuted for having been loyal to the wrong government or having been in the wrong army, that that was a rather separate, other concern. Now, the fear and the reasons why there would have existed fear for returning is, of course, also in this case seems to be not exactly the same as the other matter; that is, whether sufficient efforts were made to investigate and prosecute war crimes that may have been committed. If you would keep that -- Mr. Misetic is nodding no. So, therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's just -- we actually talked about this last night because this discussion came up in court yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And we are completely confused as to what the issue is, and I am still completely confused as to what the issue is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's ask, then, Mrs. Rehn whether you consider this two, separate problems and whether you could tell us what bothers you more than the other or less than the other.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My concern, of course, in this specific case of the Operation Storm was what happened to those who went out. My concerns -- and it was not my mandate to talk about what happened earlier, what was wrong and right before that, what the Serbs did to Croatia when taking over this Krajina region. And my concern was about what happened to the Serbs during Operation Storm when they found or feared to stay whatever security they could perhaps have had to stay. But they escaped to different neighbouring countries, 180.000 of them or something else, it will never be stated exactly. And what kind of fears they had to return back home, not only the neighbours and their attitude, but their security. Then this question of amnesty law, that will it make them unsafe, what will really happen. They didn't understand who, who was covered by the amnesty and who was not, however clear it might have been. So they are two different cases, you are absolutely right, Your Honour. But if this is confusing, let's be all accused then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I think it would not be appropriate to enter into a full debate between Chamber and counsel on these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The problem, of course, Your Honour, is that while the witness is still here to the extent that there is an issue that we can clarify with her, it is perhaps something we can discuss before the next break so that she's not present in the room. However, I don't see -- I think we're talking about apples and oranges. The issue being raised by the Defence is not what her motivation was or the motivation of the international community. The issue is whether a general amnesty law was passed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I think that -- let's discuss it at a later stage and in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think I misunderstand you. The issue might be, as you say, apples and oranges, fine. I thought that the witness was talking about apples, and that you moved on with the oranges. That's my concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have an opportunity at a later stage to see what my concern and what my problem is, then we do that in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I guess the only thing I would add to that before I move on is that we're sort of talking in the abstract about this. The bar table submission, I think, will make it clear when we file it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And we will do it as quickly as we can, given the amount of translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, no problem. You may have noted that the witness very much emphasized that she, although knowing about the abstract, very much wanted to look at the concrete as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Right. And I know she had -- the witness had said she's not a lawyer, so that's another of the reasons why we want to enter these laws at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps good for her.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I can't study now in a short while the full --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, please proceed, and I hope we don't have the full fruit basket within the next half-hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Me either, Your Honour. Thank you. If we could please call up P639.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Rehn, I'll submit, while we're waiting for the document to get up on the screen, this is your report of 7 November 1995 to the United Nations, and I wanted to ask you a few questions about this document. It's true, is it not, that every time you submitted a report regarding Croatia as you are -- during the course of your term, Croatia submitted a written response to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have already stated that that was one of the reasons for the reports, to get the governments in the former Yugoslavia to react in a positive way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that at least, as far as you're concerned, the Croatian government did act in a positive way to your reports?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. And I have paid a lot of credit to them in my reports, grateful for the cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You did begin on page 6 of your report, and feel free to let me know when you have that in front of you. If you have the hard copy, Mrs. Rehn, it might be easier for you to follow the hard copy because if we go from page to page, it takes a little longer on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's at tab 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay, I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. If you go to page 6, paragraph 13. You did discuss, at least in your first report, some of the history of what happened in former Sectors North and South before Operation Storm, correct --

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: -- as a historical context? In the middle of that paragraph 13, it states: "First, almost the entire Croatian population was forced to leave both former Sectors as a consequence of serious human rights violations committed against them by the de facto Serb authorities. Secondly, Serbian refugees and displaced persons from other parts of Croatia came to reside in these territories. @despite all efforts, neither the United Nations Protection Force, UNPROFOR, in the former Yugoslavia, nor the United Nations Confidence Restoration Operation in Croatia, UNCRO, was able to facilitate the return of Croatian refugees and displaced persons to these territories, even as an international presence was not able to provide effective protection for the remaining non-Serbian population in that area." And I'll pause for the translation. Did I go slow enough?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're the one who reads so slowly that the translation's able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The Croatian government responded to that in P684 [sic]. That's at several parts, but what I wanted to do at this point was just go over to P684 [sic], if we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And, counsel, if you could give me the tab number for Ms. Rehn, so she could follow in the hard copy, I would be grateful. Hand keep your hand on that page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you referring to P640, by any chance?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: 648. If I said 684, it's my dyslexia. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Tab 16, Mrs. Rehn.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Tab 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 6, which I believe is the second -- on the second page of this report. While we realize now after your testimony that your focus was on occurrences during and after Operation Storm, the Croatian government responds that there were approximately more than -- or there were more than 600 civilians who were killed by Serb paramilitaries during the UNPROFOR/UNCRO mandate in a time where there was technically no war in Croatia; correct?
Oh, yes, it's stated here. And you have, of course, to remember that the Special Rapporteur here means, Tadeusz Mazowiecki, and not Elisabeth Rehn.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct, understood. Now, if we go back to your report, and if you -- I'm going to try to do not too much going back and forth. But since P648 is a response to your response which is P639, if you could keep your hand on one of them while you're flipping back and forth. If we could go to page 8, paragraph 22, there's a discussion of information provided by the Croatian authorities on 30 August, indicating that during Operation Storm, 526 Serbs where are killed, 116 of them civilians; that 211 Croatian soldiers and policemen and 42 Croatian civilians were killed; and that 907 persons were detained for investigation, 704 of whom are still in detention. What I wanted -- the reason for the comparison of the two is I wanted to ask you: Did you have any information in your report that would dispute, at least from the Croatian authority side, how many persons were killed during the course of Operation Storm, as listed in paragraph 22?

I definitely can't say that this would be wrong or right because that was an information that we have got, and it's impossible for me to have numbers and figures here now. For me then, it was most interesting with those cases that we raised and never got a final answer from the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. And the reason I point that out is during the UNPROFOR/UNCRO mandate when there was technically no armed combat, there was 600 civilians killed. During the course of military -- in Croatia under Serb occupation, and during the course of armed combat, as noted in paragraph 22, at least from the Croatian authority side, less people were killed in a time-frame during the course of the war. Now, my question to you is, with respect to the number of people killed, I think you said you did not have any other information at your disposal that would be able to prove or disprove that number; correct?
Of this during my time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.
Of course, what happened earlier is something that I was not even asking for the configuration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go back to P648, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The first page of P648 is actually the cover letter from deputy prime minister and minister of foreign affairs, Dr. Mate Granic. Had you had a chance to meet Dr. Granic, Ms. Rehn?
We have -- we have reported on several meetings with Mr. Granic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I just -- you knew who he was; correct?
Absolutely. I met him many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The second-last paragraph of his letter states: "I avail myself of the opportunity to reiterate the unwavering commitment of my government to the overall development of the democratic system, rule of law, and human rights in Croatia." Now, having had a chance to meet Dr. Granic and talk with him, did you believe him that that's actually how he felt when he wrote this?

Dr. Granic had a very good team of people around him, and I remember well that especially Mrs. Simunovic was very devoted to human rights who was his assistant on the human rights side. I believe that he tried and he wanted to make it right. I'm not sure that he could fulfil everything that he promised. But as I said, we met several times. He was always available when I asked for a meeting, and that was, of course, something that I appreciated very much. He had a real dialogue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did it seem to you that from your perspective in dealing with Dr. Granic that the Croatian government through its foreign affairs minister had a commitment to try to make things better and right?

I have mentioned earlier and I mention it again that when I insisted on renewals in the system like the Ombudsman, it was immediately taken forward and there was also other steps taken. And I must say that in their answers to my reports, we always got something new and positive that was also meant with the reports. You have to remember that a human rights reporter must be totally objective, neutral, and just look to what is really happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Understood. And, with that, you need to determine the intent of someone and what they're trying to do as well, don't you?
Sorry. Can you repeat yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. When you look and evaluate what a country is doing, you try to look and see what the intent is of the people who are trying to accomplish those goals, do you not?
Of course, I'm looking to the intent, but even more to the results.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. And we can say, at least as far as refugee return that we've heard of, the results have been substantial over the course of time, have they not?
Yes. But not during the time from 1995 to 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And --
And that is what I'm covering.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Understood. The paragraph 10 of your -- of Dr. Granic's response -- actually, I'm sorry, not paragraph 10. Paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, for the record, that's P648.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 17, Dr. Granic provides some statistical information on the damage that Croatia suffered during the war and occupation, and also discusses to some extent the fires that occurred on the territory after Operation Storm. Now, at least at this point in time, there is no accurate number that you -- you've talked about some numbers in terms of homes that were destroyed in that territory. There is no accurate number that can give us a figure as to how many homes were destroyed as a result of either arson or as a result of conduct by persons after the war?
Yes. We have still these 5.000 estimated that we have been talking about already earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You see the Croatian government here has a different number, which I would assume you would think was low, that there was some houses that were caught on fire as a consequence of war operations, and at least as of this -- date of this report, 715 were partly or totally destroyed by having been intentionally set on fire. Obviously, there's a huge discrepancy between 715 and 5.000, but would you agree with me that an accurate number would have to be somewhere in between those two?

That's possible, that's possible. But I don't -- I don't take any kind of strong standpoint on this, as it's impossible for me to verify here, as it was not even then when the questions were actual for and we dealt with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Understood. Ms. Rehn, when you were on your tour, did you ever take any pictures of anything that you saw?
There are a lot of pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That you took?
Private, private photos, yes, especially my security major took pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not it was a policy of yours as Special Rapporteur to photograph areas that you went to see for official purposes?
These pictures are very private, and they have not been used at all for anything else. It was -- it was a documentation of one period of my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I understand that, Mrs. Rehn. I was just asking you if there was any official policy on whether or not Special Rapporteur would photograph --
No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

Definitely not, at least not anything that was told to me. Just because of the freedom of the Special Rapporteur, there were really cases like in Bosnia and Herzegovina when I went against the explicit orders of the United Nations mission to go to a place that was dangerous, and I have even photos from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Rehn, would you agree with me that at least during your time in Croatia, no one ever prevented you from going out to see what you really wanted to see?

I must say that it was really a luxury to be a Special Rapporteur on human rights in this whole territory -- in that whole territory, because even in Serbia and Montenegro, I got the right to walk around wherever I wanted. I got it from President Milosevic directly, and that was something my predecessor didn't have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure, I understand that. I specifically asked you about Croatia, though.
Yes, of course. But I want to make it clear that there were no limits, limitations, for me in the territory of my mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If you take a look, Ms. Rehn, at paragraph 18 of P648, again, Dr. Granic in his response to your report provides some statistical information about criminal acts of grand theft. And he notes in his last sentence: " ... some data from the Special Rapporteur's report are impossible to verify because they are incomplete and vague." It's fair to state that his observation regarding your report on verification is accurate, is it not?

There were case, like the Grubori case, that is in one way destroying a lot of what he is saying because there were clear verification. There was a correspondence between us, and I never could get and have not get until this day any kind of explanation of who were the perpetrators. So that took a little bit out of the competence of what he == or accuracy of what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure, I understand. My question was related to criminal acts of grand theft which is noted in paragraph 18, not anything else. It's true, is it not, that with respect to the 1.054 criminal acts of grand theft that have been recorded in the liberated territories, there were some data from the Special Rapporteur that were impossible to verify because they are incomplete and vague; correct?

It's quite possible because, as I have told so many times before here, that the data were collected by my staff through discussions with other UN agencies and others and by what they found out themselves, and it's possible that in some cases it could have been difficult to follow up for the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If you go to the next page, Ms. Rehn -- Mrs. Rehn, I'm sorry.
Oh, you can call me whatever you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Paragraph 22, there's a discussion that there are -- from Dr. Granic in his response that there are some 3 million land-mines scattered throughout Croatia. I mean, that's a significant obstacle in many instances to getting people to return, is it not?
Yes, that is something I have been able to feel myself when travelling around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to P650, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, this is your report of December of 1995. This is your second report; correct?
That must be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, for the record, that -- although it was marked as P650, it's an exhibit tendered before under P477, and it was corrected this morning. So the exhibit number is P477.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that, counsel. I appreciate that. As I said before, math is not my strong suit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we go to page --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You can find it, Ms. Rehn, at tab 19.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have it here now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could please go to page 5, and in paragraph 18, you actually cite Dr. Granic's response in the report itself; correct?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And there are some additional information which you note in paragraph 19, which says: "On 16 November," and I'm looking at the fourth line going into the fifth line of paragraph 19. "On 16 November, a senior Croatian police official reported to the United Nations that three Croatian soldiers had been arrested in connection with looting, intimidation, and harassment of civilians in the area. The three had then been transferred to the Karlovac military headquarters. United Nations observers have witnessed incidents where property has been confiscated from looters by Croatian police." Now, was that reported to you by the UN military observers? Can you give me any more definition on who the United Nations observers were who that you are referring to there?
No. It could have been whoever of all the different agencies, all the different organizations who were operating there, so I can't give you any clearance on who exactly this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 20, you note on the third line from the bottom going into the second line from the bottom: "Croatian authorities have made efforts to confiscate and return property, but it appears that these have been insufficient to address the magnitude of the problem." Can you give us any indication as to what you mean by that they may have been insufficient?

In the paragraph before, there is the mentioning of that -- that property has been confiscated from looters by Croatian police, but that nothing more has been then happening to these; and that if my memory is telling me rightly, that what happened to this property in the very end was quite unclear for our observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So you were referring to that specific case, not anything in general?
No, I think this is quite general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you. If we could go to page 10 of this report, Mrs. Rehn, please, and if you look at paragraph 41.
Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to start another theme, and I don't know if it's a good time to break now or should we break early.

utterances.text: Would you give us an indication how much time you would still need, so it can give us an indication whether we should break now or in ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I would say 20 minutes to half an hour at most.

utterances.text: And, Mahindaratne, how much time would you need?

utterances.text: Then you gave us a time estimate yesterday, Mr. Kuzmanovic, which was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I thought it was an hour to an hour and a half, Your Honour, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Hour to an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I know you know how much time I've taken; I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll check about the information. Of course, we'd like to conclude the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Most definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- testimony of Mrs. Rehn. Well, it depends on how many questions we would have. Then there's no need at this moment to continue because you'll not finish before the break. However, Mr. Misetic, you're on your feet. You have on your mind the other matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before the witness leaves in case there's something that needs to be put to her about the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we will, first of all, ask the usher to escort Mrs. Rehn out of the courtroom. And after that, Mr. Kuzmanovic, you are encouraged to see whether you could finish in certainly not more than 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, we're discussing the matter in the absence of -- as far as I'm concerned, I see that there are two topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. It may be helpful if I explain what I was cross-examining on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- and that may alleviate some of the -- at least my confusion. At page 18, lines 3 to 25 of yesterday's transcript, Ms. Mahindaratne tried to introduce to the witness the issue of whether the general amnesty act was intended to cover only the act of rebellion or all crimes committed in connection with the armed conflict. The purpose of my cross-examination was to show through the witness that the act was intended to be as broad as possible, to cover all crimes as possible. The fact that incidental to that inquiry was the issue of the underlying policy reason from the international community was to make it as broad as possible for Serbs was incidental to my cross-examination. The main issue being what was the intent of having the law as broad as possible. The other issues that have now been introduced -- so when we say apples to oranges, I thought it was apples to apples as to what I was crossing in response to directly to something that had been raised direct examination. The other issues now that the Trial Chamber has I'm not as clear on what the -- where the miscommunication is between on what I intended to show on cross and what issues were raised in response to my cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I may be confused by the sequence of the examination. I think that the amnesty law immediately followed concerns expressed by the witness on no prosecution for war crimes. Now, it is clear that war crimes - I would understand that easily to be war crimes, crimes against humanity, so international crimes - are to be excluded from the amnesty law in any case. To what extent theft and other common crimes are excluded is, of course, another matter. But I thought that the witness expressed some concerns about international crimes, to say so, not being prosecuted, and that the issue of what was exactly covered by the amnesty law is a different issue. As long as that is clear, I have no further problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I agree with that as long as it's clear that we will be addressing the issue, because the issue of international crimes in this context is also an issue that needs to be further developed in the course of this trial and the classification of them and, more importantly, who it is in the Croatian system that's responsible for making the determination as to whether something is an international crime as opposed to a domestic crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: These are all issues to be developed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And who are prosecuted for crimes allegedly committed, in what context and what period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct. That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just explain. The reason I explored this issue with the witness is based on the bar table submission made by the Defence. We were alerted to this line of argument, and that is the reason I explored this area with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At this moment, I do not feel that there is great confusion, not even small confusion. So we can leave the matter, as far as I'm concerned, as it is at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as the Bench is concerned, we'll have a break and we'll resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we please have P600. I know the 65 ter number is 309. I'm almost certain it's P600. But if I'm wrong, I'm sure Mr. Registrar will correct me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's at tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to the second page of that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, this is another response from Minister Granic and the Croatian government regarding your report to the Security Council. And if we could go to page 4, there is a response on page 4 regarding measures taken against individuals and groups to perpetrated crimes in the liberated areas after Operation Storm. And under that same heading on page 5, in the first full paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, the bottom right-hand corner on the left document, it says "3." It's actually page 5 of the document itself. It might not be page 5 of the exhibit. I will say page 5 of the document itself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: There's some statistical information, again, provided in response to your report about criminal proceedings underway in military and civilian courts against 1.005 persons who stand accused of having committed crimes during and after Operation Storm. And there's a discussion of what stages some of these proceedings are in, where they are taking place, and also there's an annex that's appended which I don't know if it's appended to this specific 62 [sic] ter or P document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go very last page, which is page 10 of P600.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, the document I have in front of me -- oh, no, that must be a mistake. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Just to ask the registrar, is there another page beyond this last page 10 to this exhibit? Okay. If we could go to that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got a 31-page document from what I see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Then the document I have must not be complete. I'll just refer -- if we could call up 3D00-1588, please -- I'm sorry, I'm sorry. Don't call that up. I'll stick with this particular document. That's the next document. My confusion. I apologise. We will go back to this same document that we're on, page 7 on the lower right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: There is also a discussion on return of refugees and displaced persons, which states as of 10 January 1996, there were little under 3.000 requests for the return of just over 4.500 Serbs who left, and that a description of the processing that's done of 50 files per day. And if you can look at the following page, page 8, there's a notation in the first full paragraph, the fourth line down, which -- in which Dr. Granic is explaining that there are 180.000 displaced persons within Croatia and 192.500 refugees on the territory of the Republic of Croatia. So, in addition to dealing with attempts for processing of returnees of Serbs, they had several hundred thousand displaced people and refugees that they had to deal with, which is understandable in that situation, is it not, Mrs. Rehn?
Yes. And I also pointed out in my earlier statements that you have to remember that there is -- was a great amount of refugees and displaced persons within the -- Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And despite the fact that there was some bureaucratic obstacles with regard to the return of Serb refugees, there was also a huge problem of dealing with the people who were already displaced within Croatia; correct?
Yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If you look further on this same page, there is a discussion that the Croatian government terminated the dead-line by which Serbs who had left had to return to reclaim their property. So, at least from that standpoint, a potential bureaucratic obstacle was removed; correct?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we go to page 10 of this same document --
But there is not said how much they terminated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll submit to you that for the record there, the termination of the dead-line means that the dead-line was eliminated completely from the law. So there was no dead-line as of the date of this lay, 17 January 1996. At least, you don't have any information to the contrary that there was a dead-line beyond this law, do you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Kuzmanovic is reading evidence into the record. He said he submits it for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That means that it is not evidence. He gives his personal opinion about the information he has in order to -- the Chamber will, of course, ignore that as evidence, but it might assist at this moment, even if we do not have this law immediately at hand, the version of the 17th of January, 1996, that Mr. Kuzmanovic leads the witness in this respect. But it's certainly not to be considered to be evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. Your Honour, I think that document is already in evidence. I don't have the particular D number right now, but I will before the end of the day get it to Your Honours regarding this law. It's already in evidence through Mr. Galbraith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, we would have to look very carefully at the retroactive --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- retroactive effect of abolishing a time-limit. I don't have that clearly on my mind at this moment. So, Mr. Kuzmanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Just to end the discussion regarding this topic, Mrs. Rehn. You were not aware at all, were you, of a specific dead-line other than the -- of a new dead-line that was set as a result of this particular law, were you?

In my reports, I have several times referred to this 90 days dead-line. So that has been quite obvious that is one of the matters I have been especially been criticising from for the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Were you aware at any time that the Croatian parliament passed a law terminating or eliminating that dead-line?

I can't -- I can't just recognise this. But, of course, I got the response from the Croatian government, the paper we now -- the document we now are dealing with. So then I knew or perhaps I knew already earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 10 of this same document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: There was some document, both today and yesterday, on the amnesty law. And the first full paragraph discusses that: "President Tudjman pardoned by eliminating criminal charges against 455 persons of Serb ethnicity detained during and immediately after Operation Storm. These were persons facing criminal charges before the military courts in Zagreb, Split, and Karlovac for the criminal act of armed rebellion ..." Does this clarify for you at all the issue of amnesty from President Tudjman at least as from December 31st, 1995?

It was certainly known by me then, but what was worrying me was, of course, the reaction of the Serbs who wanted to return because it was not clear for them: Are they included or outside, what will happen to them, do they have the chance of meeting charges when and if they return.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you please call 3D00-1749 to the screen. Your Honour, we have a partial draft translation of this document. This will be part of our bar table submission when it's completely translated. But for purposes of hopefully clarifying in the Court's mind this law on general amnesty and the description for what is and what is not amnestied, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I may, I am sorry to rise to my feet, I believe we tendered the law. It's Exhibit D680.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The same one, counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry I missed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there's no need, I take it, and that you withdraw your --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- request. Please proceed.

utterances.text: I would like to call up 3D00-1588.
