What I noted was not in evidence were the last five pages of the -- this 3D document, which is the survey of criminal proceedings. And if I could ask, Mr. Registrar, to go to the fifth-from-the-last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, this was another document written via Dr. Granic in response to another report of yours, and this particular response is dated 14 March 1996. And I would like to turn your attention to the survey of criminal proceedings underway, which is a table listing perpetrators of criminal acts or the kinds of criminal acts after Operation Storm. And it's further divided up on the following pages as to where these actions are occurring, in addition to other statistical data in response to your queries. Do you recall receiving this survey at all?
Oh, yes. And I believe it's included in the documents we have here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, I could not find it on e-court or as appended to the original exhibit. Was it appended to the original exhibit, this survey?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is appended, yes, table 1 to the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Then I will not offer it as a separate exhibit. I just wanted to make sure. At least from what I could find, I couldn't find it appended to the exhibit, Your Honour. I apologise for that delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You also said this is further elaborated in the pages to follow. That's not something I found there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. What I meant was the survey was an attachment to the report and the previous pages discussed the survey. So it was my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The survey discusses, does it not, the number -- and we had previously seen the number of 1.005 criminal proceedings listed on the bottom of that first page of the survey.
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Then it discusses what kind of criminal proceedings are being pursued, at least on the page following as an example on the second page. If we could go to the county court of Split, for example, which is in Sector South, former Sector South, proceedings are underway against 28 persons as follows, and it discusses what they were charged with, the offence of aggravated larceny. Now, were you made aware at any time of the complete number of persons who were prosecuted and/or convicted during this time-frame, other than through these reports?

I cannot remember this because, of course, this was one way of answering the requests I have been doing and putting to the authorities, and all these figures were most welcome and the clarifications were most welcome to the office of the Special Rapporteur. But what then has been told later on is impossible for me to just remember here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Understood. And just for clarification, Mrs. Rehn, the other -- for the benefit of the Chamber, the Sibenik, Zadar county courts were also courts which dealt with matters in former Sector South. Were you aware of that at all?
I have this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to P638, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And that is your report dated 14 March of 1996, Mrs. Rehn.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd be grateful if we could get a tab for her, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If you could look, Mrs. Rehn, page 19, paragraph 73 of this report, there is a discussion on that page about how many Serb refugees have been approved, 2.100 out of 5.600 requests received. And there was an indication that considerably more Croatian Serbs would like to return to Croatia. It was -- was it your experience that even though the approval process started out slowly, it gradually gained speed over the course of your time as Special Rapporteur?
It started, of course, immediately, but very slowly and very much, of course, depending on the resistance from the villagers where -- to which it is returns will be directed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, just for the record, in order to avoid whatever confusion, you referred to P638, but that same document has changed identity and is D669.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could go, please, to P645.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's tab 13, Mrs. Rehn.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I know that there was some concern you had, Mrs. Rehn, regarding evictions from military Ministry of Defence flats. This particular portion of your report, if you look at paragraph 25, is the Croatian government's response to the procedure involved. And I'll wait until you get there, if you let me know when you're there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, has there been any communication between Prosecution and Defence about the relevance of the eviction of military apartments? Because I thought that this was not very much in the core of -- is it of any relevance for the Prosecution's case?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Not with regard to military apartments, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I was only trying to demonstrate another aspect, but that will be argued later on. We don't have to deal with military apartments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So whatever we think about that will not in any way influence --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Right. So as long as I'm clear that the issue of military apartments and the evictions of people from military apartments and that methodology is not an issue in this trial, then I will not go over it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is not for demonstrative purposes you could do without, or you could --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is true that in that report that there was a reference to violence. And in the minutes, Mr. Jarnjak refers to the ability of the civilian police to deal with that issue as opposed to the military police, and that's what I tried to demonstrate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's competence of the police, that's the only relevant issue there, and not exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, I leave it to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- whether you feel any need to further explore the eviction of military apartments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we may deal with that in a bar table submission rather than waste time on that now. I will move on. I wanted to make the Court aware regarding the various laws and the dead-lines which were admitted through Ambassador Galbraith: D422 was the 90-day time-limit; D425 was the constitutional court making that unconstitutional; and D424 was the law where the -- D425 and D422 were the two exhibits, Your Honour, that dealt with that issue. I will move to P640.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's tab 6, Mrs. Rehn.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Page 15, paragraph 50. Let me know, Mrs. Rehn, when you're there.
Yes, I'm here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 50 notes that: "According to the Croatian office for displaced persons and refugees, some 12.000 Serb refugees have received permission to return to the country as of 12 October 1996, mostly on the basis of family reunification or proof of citizenship." Now, that's, of course, a number that's from your previous report gone up several thousand; correct?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So the bureaucratic obstacles, although are -- which were still perhaps in place were improving?
Yes. Of course, they were improving, and all the time I could state that steps forward are taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, we've got additional information regarding -- I'll strike that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Why don't we move to P651, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Tab 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's your final report of January 14, 1998 on paragraph 29, which is page 9, and I appreciate your patience in struggling through the documents, Mrs. Rehn.
I have seen them before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: In your final report, you note on paragraph 29: "After more than two years of observing human rights trends in Croatia, the Special Rapporteur is of the opinion that while more still needs to be accomplished, there are good reasons for optimism for the future." And then later on, in that same paragraph, you discuss statistical information received from the Government of Croatia that says: " ... as of October 1997, a total of 5.580 criminal proceedings had been carried out in relation to the military operations carried out in the former Sectors North and South," and further discussions of at what stages those proceedings are. Now, when you left or after you issued your final report, Mrs. Rehn, was -- you still were dealing with Dr. Granic primarily from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs; correct?

When I left my mission as Special Rapporteur, of course, I was totally concentrated on my new mission. That was a much -- that was a UN mission directly as the SIG chief or UNMIK in Bosnia and Herzegovina. But I was dealing with the leading team. The international team from Bosnia-Herzegovina was invited by President Tudjman then, Mr. Granic was present in year 1998/1999 sometime, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. And President Tudjman was still president of Croatia at that time, was he not?
Yes. Otherwise, he should not have been inviting us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: One final area I wanted to cover, Mrs. Rehn, relates to the issue of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hope an area which will not take one or two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It will not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I encouraged you 25 minutes, it's now 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm just looking for my D document here, Your Honour. 3D00-1689.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, I know you had a question about the nature and extent of what people were being amnestied for. This is the December 30th amnesty declaration of President Tudjman. We have a partial draft translation. It's 47 pages long. And you will see that the first gentleman is -- who was charged with armed insurgency was noted to be exempt from criminal persecution; and the same thing for the last particular person, Mr. Babic, also exempt from criminal prosecution and the charge was armed insurgency. So I don't know if that clears up your recollection or potential confusion, but I wanted to make sure that you were aware on what those charges were and how they were exempted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to offer this into evidence, and I will be done.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Information taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask specific attention, I have not checked the whole of the translation, but that someone is exempt from criminal "persecution" comes as a surprise in a state document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's probably supposed to be "prosecution."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please have a proper look at the language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will tender it, and I will be completed. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this becomes Exhibit number D693.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D693 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for the extra time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am sorry for the housekeeping matter. We've been trying to find this issue Mr. Kuzmanovic raised about and exhibit not being appended. It was 3D00-1588, and I'm not sure if that exhibit has been admitted into evidence by the Prosecution because --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The chart is attached to the exhibit that was tendered by the Prosecution. It is at page -- well, I can't recall the exact page, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that's the 33-page document?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The chart and the explanation are found in the later stages of this. I think the chart is table 1 attached to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can we have the exhibit number, though, for the entire exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think it's table 1, and in the exhibit itself is the 26th page out of 31. Ms. Mahindaratne, do you have any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you try to conclude within 13 minutes, so that the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- has an opportunity to ask additional questions as well --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to the extent not already put to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call document number D669, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, in fact, you have been questioned extensively about the general amnesty. If you want to follow the hard copy, it's at tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if I could ask, Mr. Registrar, to take us to page 19. So that we don't waste time, I'll quickly refer you to the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, at paragraph 72, you report in the following matter: "On 30 December 1995, the President of Croatia issued a decree granting amnesty to 451 Krajina Serbs accused of 'armed rebellion' for their alleged military support of the so-called 'Republic of Serb Krajina.' This decision of the Croatian Government was noted with appreciation by the Security Council in a statement by the President dated 8 January 1996. Nevertheless, the Special Rapporteur is of the opinion that a general amnesty, which has not yet been decreed, is a condition sine qua non for the return of Croatian Serbs, who will otherwise fear prosecution for having served in the army of so-called 'Republic Serb Krajina.'" Now, if I could also take you, Mrs. Rehn, to page 26 at paragraph 109. In your recommendations, you recommend as follows: "In order to build confidence and provide security, the Croatian authorities should increase policing and humanitarian projects in the former Sectors. A general amnesty should be decreed for all former combatants of the so-called 'Republic of Serb Krajina,' and the return of Croatian Serb refugees now in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and elsewhere should be facilitated." Now, whom did you intend and whom did the international community intend to be the beneficiary of this general amnesty that you were proposing? And if you could be brief since I'm running out of time.

Yes, I will be brief. It's my interest to be brief. It's my clear opinion that we thought of the Serbs that have escaped for some or another reason during the Operation Storm, and to make it possible not to have an obstacle through this, to get general amnesty. So it was directed to the Serbs. Of course, what has been raised about that law must be the same to all nationalities is, of course, clear. But for my part, I was thinking of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And whatever group the persons, beneficiaries, belonged to, did you intend the acts that amnesty would relate to be common crimes such as theft or looting? Is that what was intended, or did you intend it to be prosecution for participation --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's leading, Your Honour, again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, I'll leave it at this, Mr. President. I've asked the question now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The question was already leading, so I'd ask that it be stricken or at least be reformulated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me check.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I rephrase, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, one second, please. Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, did you understand this general amnesty to include amnesty from prosecution of common crimes such as theft?
It's very difficult for me to even --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You object against the question on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: On what is she specifically referring to? I mean, now we need to know -- the law wasn't passed until August. She's crossing her with a document from March. She's asking her opinion of a law that wasn't passed until six months earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that Ms. Mahindaratne was asking not about a specific -- yes, now you're referring to the law. Was what you had in mind as far as an amnesty was concerned, did you have in mind that the aim should be to prevent prosecution of those who had actively participated or were members of the armed forces, called often the rebellion forces; or that it should be wider to include not only this rebellion-type participating in the armed forces, but going beyond that, common crimes such as theft and others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for making it clear for -- the question quite clear for me. With my democratic background, it would have been impossible for me to ask for amnesty for crimes, common crimes. It was a question just of those who were involved in the battles of -- in the Krajina. So my opinion, at least, is that we - and I especially - were talking about excluding, of course, crimes from amnesty. It was a question of a war that took -- and fighting that took place, and that you should not as a simple soldier be put into trial because of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that having been a soldier in the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in the wrong army, in the rebellion army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the wrong army or whatever army. There are many wrong armies.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, if I could quickly call document number P639.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, that's at tab 5, your 7th November report. If you could look at paragraph 41, you were questioned about your report at paragraph 4, and it says: "However, the Special Rapporteur points out that a couple thousand Croatian Serb refugees are already waiting in Hungary for return and are being prevented from doing so by various bureaucratic missions instituted by Croatian officials." Now, at the time you wrote this report, did you receive that information as if those persons were at that time waiting, or did you perceive that they had been there for some time? What was the information? Was it contemporaneous information, or was it -- did you relate it to a different time-frame?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's leading and it's four different options to the witness on which option she wishes to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you mention all the options, then you're still leading at what the options are, and at the same time the reason why you should not lead the witness disappears at the same time. Ms. Mahindaratne --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it was because I'm running out of time, and I just wanted to narrow down the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, the more options you give, the more you run out of time. Could you try to rephrase the question. I mean, if there's damage, it's done already. We're not going to strike this from the record. To the extent you've understood the question by Ms. Mahindaratne, could you give a brief answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I got the information from several sources of my staff and others that there are Serb refugees from Croatia who are waiting, who are trying to get the permission to come back again, and to claim for their property. I can't say if they had been there from the whole -- the whole time or if there was something that had happened just now that they have gone over borders to Hungary and waited that way to come back to Croatia. I'm sorry, I can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, you took over as Special Rapporteur on 27th September 1995; that's correct, isn't it?
Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you were questioned about the property laws. On the same page, if you look at paragraph 38 and 39, you deal with property laws. And in paragraph 39, you say: "It remains unclear what the status of the property is after the 90 days are over, even though it has been stipulated that the ownership of unclaimed property will be dealt with by a special law." Did you ever understand as to what happened if an owner did not return within the 90 days stipulated time and claimed that property, as to what would happen to that property?

That was what we were very much worried about what will happen to it, because we knew that the Croatian authorities needed property, homes, for those many hundred thousands of displaced and also refugees in Croatia. But, of course, for us it was important to know that people could rely upon that they don't lose the right to their own property. I can't just answer this now more than this that it was what we were worried about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have only one last question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And what happened if the claimants or the owners returned within three months, did they -- as you know the law or as according to your information, were they given their property back immediately or was there some other condition which was required?

In principle, in theory, they should give -- get their property back. But as I have been describing, there were cases that I witnessed myself that people have come back, they had the rights to the property, but somebody else was staying in their home, and they couldn't just get them out because they didn't have anywhere to go. It was a complicated situation altogether.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And I read this last sentence to you. You read: "Furthermore, even if the owner does return within the dead-line, his or her property will not be restored until the Croatian citizen to whom the property has been given receives another appropriate property for possession and use."
Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The witness gave her answer, she wasn't satisfied with the answer, now we're reading from the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have not heard the question Ms. Mahindaratne wanted to put. She said I'll read the last sentence to you, that's what she did, and then I expect a question to follow. But I do not know what this question is about, whether the witness remembers ever to have read this text before, or whether it was she who drafted it or one of her staff. I haven't heard a question yet. What would your question be, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And that would be my last.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may understand that Mr. Misetic would strongly object against the question, Is this what your actual answer would be, because then it would not be leading but it would become a university example of leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I had a question, but Mr. Misetic did not give me the option.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please put your question which is expected not to be a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, and what was the basis for what you have reported there about the property being restored to the owner if the Croatian occupant was given another suitable property? Now, what was the basis? Was that included in the law or was it based on information that you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you start leading, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were doing so well in just asking what's the basis for that, and then you started to give a few propositions to the witness, which Mr. Misetic wouldn't like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I feel like a jack-in-the-box, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But I must say that I have fallen out from this too in the sense that this exact legislation and what will happen then was not clear for me, and I counted on that in the moment the apartment was released for the proper owner, they will get it. But I'm not sure that it happened every time. But this is my answer on this, and that's certainly not satisfactory. But I don't want to make any kind of different statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That concludes re-examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Gwaunza has -- Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Two short questions, and I will do it in less than a minute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I think we now give priority to the Bench's questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll see whether there's still time left. Judge Gwaunza

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Yes, Mrs. Rehn, if I could take you back to your report of 7 November 1995.
Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Page 9, paragraph 25, specifically paragraph 25(c), where you stated that: "On 12 August, it was reported that a number of elderly persons were burnt to death in the village of Komic [phoen]." I just want to ask whether you had recall any more details about this incident.

Your Honour, I'm very sorry, but I can't recall more about this. There were several, several brutal murders during that time of civilians, and we, of course, especially looked into them. But I have mentioned, but nobody else is interested in that, the Grubori case several times. And that was something I was very much dealing with since I never got the proper answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, I can tell you that in this courtroom, the Grubori incident has received a lot of attention until now. It just --
That makes me very pleased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, yes, but it's fine. Judge Gwaunza.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since we have no further questions and since Mr. Misetic promised that he would need one minute for two questions. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, was it your intention in advocating for a general amnesty law that the Government of Croatia in 1996 could charge Serbs for, let's say, stealing a refrigerator or burning a house between 1991 and 1995?
They will definitely not be able to charge, I think I already answered that question, that my Nordic democracy is really not allowing amnesty from criminal acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So the answer is your belief is that, yes, the Croatian government could continue to prosecute Serbs for stealing a refrigerator, for example?
Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is that a yes?
Yes. I have answered that already once.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Then the last question for you is: Do you think that, if that were the case, that Serbs would have felt any material difference in their ability to return to Croatia and not face prosecutions from the Croatian government to put them in jail upon their return?

Yes, absolutely, because it was an important part of these. But what they were worried about was the list that was presented. Because when you are not on a list and you have been in the combat as an ordinary combatant, then you can be worried about what will happen to you. I think we should forget about the civilian criminal acts. We should just concentrate on these that what happened during the Operation Storm and the combats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, we have a broader issues here to deal with. So the question is you've brought up the lists. You do recall that the international community, and the United Nations specifically, told the Croatian government to put together a list of 25 Serbs who could be prosecuted for war crimes, and that the rest of them were to consider themselves to be immune from prosecution before Croatian courts; isn't that correct?

I'm talking for myself. I think that we, again, must make a clear the difference between the Special Rapporteur, her capacity, and not representing the high-level international community, United Nations decisions and so on. And I find this quite important, that we keep this in mind, because it's putting me as a witness in a quite awkward situation to answer questions for the United Nations and international community, when with the background, a Special Rapporteur must have for her work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, you used 300 per cent of your time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I took something of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course, Mr. Misetic did not ask one minute to put questions, put to hear the answers well. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have a question. Just with respect to this law on temporary taking -- the taking or use of property, the law itself is D428. It's in evidence, it's translated, it's in English. So if the Court can't for itself determine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we'll not ask the witness to interpret legal texts. Mrs. Rehn, at least, yes, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for having come to The Hague and for having answered the many, many questions put to you by the parties and not that many by the Bench. I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It has been a pleasure to be working together with the four of you and the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please escort Mrs. Rehn out of the courtroom

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is one tiny procedural issue which I would like to briefly raise. For this afternoon -- for this Friday afternoon, a hearing has been scheduled, and, apparently, for practical purposes the registry has inquired into whether the accused wanted to be present or not. This was not initiated by the Chamber because the Chamber considers a hearing under Rule 54 bis the same hearing, unless specific requests are made by the state too. We have considered this hearing as just an ordinary hearing. Meanwhile, the Chamber is informed of the accused to waive their right to be present, which I understand prefer not to be present, and one accused has chosen to be present. I just put this on the record that inquiring into the matter which the Chamber might not have spontaneously done, but I do understand that there might be practical reasons for that, might create a situation in which one of the accused would say, "Well, I wasn't aware that the other would come," whatever it is. You can consider or reconsider, and I'm not encouraging you to do so. But if you want to reconsider your choice to be present or not to be present, please let the registry know as soon as possible in view of the practical implications. May I take it that certainly not later than by today this is done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we adjourn and we'll adjourn tomorrow, the 17th of July, at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon. And we'll be, Mr. Registrar, in Courtroom II where we will hear the testimony through videolink. We have the reasons for the decision on the videolink requested for Witness 172 ready. But since I do understand that for all kind of practical purposes we'll not hear that evidence anyhow, this Friday, we'll not further burden the interpreters and transcribers at this moment, but the reasons are ready. We stand adjourned until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 17th day of July, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.
